how-much-to-charge-to-install-solar-pane.text:
← Solar PV install bid calculator

How much to charge to install solar panels

Price the job from cost, then convert to dollars per watt. Do not start from a published $/W and work backwards. Two 10 kW residential arrays can differ by several thousand dollars once the roof and the electrical service are in the bid.

Open the free bid calculator

What a per-watt quote cannot see

Modules, inverters, and racking mostly scale with watts. These do not:

  • Steep pitch, tile or slate, hips and valleys, or a second array
  • A 100 A → 200 A (or 200 A → 400 A) service upgrade
  • A long AC/DC run, a trench to a detached structure, or a ground-mount pier field
  • Permit, interconnection, and utility fees that are a trip and a check, not a watt
  • A battery or backup adder sold on the same visit

If you match a cheaper $/W quote that was written for an easy composition roof and a clean 200 A panel, you are matching someone else's job, not yours.

A bid that holds together

  1. Size the array from module count × watts, not a rounded marketing kW.
  2. Time array labor as hours per kW on an easy roof, then multiply by a roof factor.
  3. Add electrical extras as their own hours and material. They do not shrink when the array is smaller.
  4. Load the wage (taxes, workers' compensation, insurance, PTO). Price from loaded labor, not take-home.
  5. Add permits, design, travel, dumpster, and lift.
  6. Recover overhead as a percent of direct cost, then set margin as a share of the customer's price.
  7. Only then look at $/W — and at the walk-away price if a closer asks you to sharpen it.

What this is not

This is not a structural stamp, an interconnection approval, a code inspection, a payback model, or tax or incentive advice. It is arithmetic on numbers you enter. Confirm layout, AHJ and utility requirements, and every invoice before you send a price.

Common questions

How much should I charge to install solar panels?

Charge from your own cost: modules, inverter, racking, BOS, crew hours times a roof-difficulty factor, electrical extras, permits, overhead, and the margin you intend to keep. Convert that price to dollars per watt at the end for comparison, not as the bid method.

Why is a dollars-per-watt quote dangerous?

Equipment scales with watts. Tile hooks, steep pitch, multiple arrays, and a 100 A to 200 A panel upgrade do not. Those extras can erase the margin on a quote that looked fine on a composition-roof job of the same size.

Does this include tax credits or utility incentives?

No. The calculator prices the install. Incentives, rebates, and tax credits are the customer's, the accountant's, or the program administrator's to apply. Do not treat the tool as a net-cost or payback determination.

No warranty. This page and the calculator are free and as-is. They are not legal, tax, financial, engineering, or electrical-code advice. You are responsible for reviewing and verifying output before relying on it. To the maximum extent permitted by law, the authors accept no liability for loss or damage from its use.

FOR SOLAR INSTALLERS

Bid the roof and the service, not the watts.

A flat dollars-per-watt quote treats a 10 kW composition-roof job with a clean 200 A panel as the same job as a 10 kW tile-roof job that needs a 100 A → 200 A upgrade. Price the array, the roof difficulty, and the electrical extras separately — then see the price, the dollars per watt, and the number below which the job loses money.

The system

Start from a common residential size, then replace module count and watts with the layout you actually drew.

The roof and the service

Roof factor multiplies array labor only. Electrical extras are a fixed hour-and-material adder — they do not get cheaper on a smaller array.

Your costs

Payroll burden covers employer taxes, workers’ compensation, liability insurance, and paid time off. Matching a cheaper per-watt quote after leaving it out is how a sold job becomes a loss.

Hand the customer a proposal

The price above is for you. This is the page you print or save as a PDF and give to the customer — your details, their details, the scope, the deposit split, and a line for them to sign. Your business details are saved on this device so you only type them once; the customer’s details are never saved.

Everything on the printed page is text you typed or a number this calculator worked out. It contains no warranty, lien, or cancellation wording — those depend on your jurisdiction and your contract, and this tool is not the place to invent them.

Where the cost goes

    Transparent arithmetic from your own inputs. Roof factors and electrical extras are common ballpark starting points, not an industry standard, a benchmark, or a guarantee. Time your own crews and replace them.

    Common questions

    Why does a dollars-per-watt quote go wrong?

    Because only part of a solar job scales with watts. Modules, racking, and balance-of-system do. Roof difficulty and electrical work do not — and they are the two lines that decide whether the job made money. Two 10 kW installs priced at the same $/W can differ by thousands: one on a clean composition roof with room in a 200 A panel, the other on tile needing a 100 A → 200 A service upgrade. This tool prices watts as watts and prices the rest as its own hours and material.

    How much does the roof type actually change labor?

    It multiplies array labor hours: composition at 4/12–6/12 is the 1.0 baseline, 7/12–9/12 is 1.18, 10/12 or steeper is 1.35, multiple arrays or hips and valleys 1.25, tile or slate 1.45 (hooks and flashings), and ground mount 1.4 (piers and trench). Metal standing seam is the one that goes down, to 0.95, because clamps beat penetrating and flashing. These are starting points for your own crew, not an industry standard — retime them from your last few jobs.

    Which electrical extras get forgotten most often?

    The panel. A supply-side or load-side tap is about 4 h and $350; a 100 A → 200 A main-panel upgrade about 8 h and $1,800; a 200 A → 400 A service upgrade about 16 h and $4,500. A new subpanel or inverter feeder, 50+ extra feet of conduit, and a trench to a detached structure each carry their own hours and material. None of these move with system size, which is exactly why a per-watt price cannot carry them.

    Where do permits, interconnection, and design go?

    They are their own flat lines — permit and interconnection, design and engineering, and travel/dumpster/lift — not a percentage of the system. Sizing, production estimates, shading analysis, incentive eligibility, and interconnection approval are all outside what this does: it is bid arithmetic on inputs you supply, not a PV design, a production model, or a claim about what any utility will approve.

    Does adding a battery just add its price?

    No, and that is why battery hours and battery material are separate fields. The hardware is one cost; the mounting, the critical-loads panel, the commissioning, and the extra inspection are labor that lands on the same crew day. Entering only the equipment cost is the same mistake as the per-watt quote, one level down.

    Why isn't a 20% margin the same as adding 20% to my cost?

    Margin here is a share of the final price — price = job cost ÷ (1 − margin) — which is how the customer's number reads and how your books read it. Overhead is a separate markup on direct cost, applied before margin and never to itself or to profit. A $18,000 cost marked up 20% is $21,600, a 16.7% margin; a 20% target margin is $22,500. No account, no upload: every figure stays in this browser, and the optional local counter records only which features were used and the day.

vs-a-flat-price-per-watt.html.text:
← Solar PV Install Bid Calculator

This calculator vs. a flat price-per-watt quote

A flat "$2.12/W installed" rate clears cost on the easy composition-roof job it was set from — and runs deeply underwater the moment the same rate is quoted on a tile roof needing a panel upgrade, or a bigger ground-mount job with a battery.

What a flat price-per-watt quote is

A flat $/W rate is the fastest number a solar company can put on a door-knock flyer or a phone quote: one rate, multiplied by system size, read back as the whole job. It is also the number homeowners compare between competing bids, since "$2.50 a watt" sounds like one job whatever the roof looks like.

The rate behind it was set for one job — a composition-shingle roof at 4/12–6/12 pitch, a single array, and a 200 A panel with room for the new breaker: this calculator's own default roof preset and "None" electrical preset. Modules, racking, and balance-of-system really do scale with watts, so a flat $/W rate prices them correctly on every job. Roof difficulty and electrical extras do not scale with watts at all — a tile roof needing hooks and flashings, or a panel that needs a service upgrade before the array can be interconnected, cost the same labor and material whether the system is 6 kW or 12 kW. A flat rate has nowhere to put that cost.

JobActual costCorrect priceQuoted at $2.12/WShortfall vs. cost
10.14 kW, composition roof, clean 200 A panel (the rate's own job)$17,186.01$21,482.52$21,482.52—
10.14 kW, tile roof, 100 A → 200 A panel upgrade$22,302.73$27,878.42$21,482.52−$820.22
12.09 kW, ground mount, 200 A → 400 A upgrade, battery$39,283.36$49,104.20$25,613.77−$13,669.59

On the rate's own job, $2.12/W clears cost with room for the full 20% target margin. Quote the same $2.12/W on the same-size job with a harder roof and a panel upgrade and the job comes in $820.22 under its own cost — a real loss before any profit, not just a thinner margin — and $6,395.90 short of the $27,878.42 the job should have been priced at. On the bigger ground-mount job with a battery, the shortfall against cost alone grows to $13,669.59.

This calculator keeps the array, the roof factor, and the electrical and battery extras as separate lines, so the rate applied to modules and racking never has to also carry a panel upgrade or a battery install. Changing the roof or electrical preset refills the starting hours and material for that choice — a field you have already hand-edited is left alone — and the price, the dollars per watt, and the walk-away number update together.

This page names no specific product or company — it compares against the generic method of quoting every job at the same flat price per watt.

Common questions

Why does a flat price-per-watt quote get the price wrong?

Because only part of a solar job scales with watts. Modules, racking, and balance-of-system cost roughly the same per watt on every roof. Roof difficulty and electrical extras do not — a tile roof needing hooks and flashings, or a panel that needs a service upgrade before the array can be interconnected, cost the same in labor and material whether the system is 6 kW or 12 kW. A flat $/W rate bakes in whatever roof and panel the rate was set from and then charges every other job as if it were that job.

What job is the flat rate actually built around?

The easiest job that walks in the door: a composition-shingle roof at 4/12–6/12 pitch, one array, and a 200 A panel with room for the new breaker — this calculator's own default roof preset and the "None" electrical preset. On that job a rate set to clear cost and margin does exactly that. It is not derived from any particular roof being quoted; it is a number set on the easy job and then reused for every job afterward.

How big does the pricing gap get on a harder or bigger job?

On this calculator's own numbers, at a $38 hourly wage, 30% payroll burden, 15% overhead, and a 20% target margin: a 10.14 kW composition-roof job with a clean 200 A panel costs $17,186.01 to run and correctly prices at $21,482.52, or $2.12/W. Quote that same $2.12/W on a same-size 10.14 kW job that instead has a tile roof and a 100 A to 200 A panel upgrade, and the job actually costs $22,302.73 to run — the flat quote comes in at $21,482.52, which is $820.22 under that job's own cost, before any profit at all, and $6,395.90 short of what it should have been priced at. Move to a 12.09 kW ground-mount job with a 200 A to 400 A service upgrade and a battery, and the same $2.12/W quotes $25,613.77 against a job that costs $39,283.36 to run — $13,669.59 under cost and $23,490.43 short of the correct price.

Is a flat price-per-watt quote ever the right way to price a job?

On the easy roof and panel it was set from, since it clears that job's own cost and margin on this calculator's own numbers. The risk is reusing the same rate once the roof or the panel changes — a tile roof with a panel upgrade is not a bigger version of the easy composition-roof job, it is a different job, and nothing about a flat $/W rate tells the installer when that line has been crossed.

Does this calculator know what to charge in my market?

No. It has no data on local module, racking, electrician, or permitting rates in your area, and it is not a PV design, a production estimate, a structural determination, or an interconnection or incentive approval. It takes the module count and wattage, roof factor, electrical and battery extras, permits, and your own wage, payroll burden, overhead, and target margin you enter, and turns that into a price for this job — the arithmetic a flat $/W rate skips, not a market survey.

Open the Solar PV Install Bid Calculator to price your own job, or read how much to charge to install solar panels.

vs-aurora-solar.html.text:
← Solar PV Install Bid Calculator

This calculator vs. Aurora Solar

Two different shapes: Aurora Solar is an account-based platform that designs a PV system remotely from satellite and LiDAR imagery and turns that design into a sales proposal. This page is a free, private, no-account worksheet for one number — whether the price for a job you have already sized, priced by watts, roof difficulty, and electrical extras, actually clears your cost and margin.

What each tool is for

Aurora Solar is a cloud-based remote design and sales platform built specifically for solar installers — it is not a generic construction or field-service tool. It models a roof in 3D from satellite and LiDAR imagery without a site visit, lays out modules and strings, generates a single-line diagram and permit-set-style drawings, and turns that design into a financial proposal a homeowner can review, run through one account across every lead a company works, on an ongoing per-seat subscription. Aurora Solar's own site is not reachable from this session to confirm today's specific feature list, plan names, or pricing, so only its well-documented identity and category are stated here: nothing about it is invented, and no dollar figure for it appears on this page.

This calculator does none of that. It does not model a roof, generate a single-line diagram, or hold a design or lead record across jobs. It starts from a system you have already sized — module count and wattage, inverter cost, racking per module, balance-of-system cost per watt, a roof-difficulty factor, labor hours per kW, electrical and battery hours and material, permitting and interconnection, design and engineering, travel and equipment, payroll burden, overhead, and the margin you intend to keep — and turns that into the job price, the price per watt, the effective hourly rate, and the walk-away number below which the job loses money, plus a printable customer proposal with a scope and price-held date. It runs free in any browser, keeps no account, and uploads nothing you type.

I need my whole sales team designing, proposing, and tracking leads from one shared account.Aurora Solar — built as an ongoing, account-based platform for exactly that job.
Do I need to create an account or sign up to use the tool?This calculator: no. Aurora Solar's tools are used through a paid, per-seat account.

Most solar installers get different value from each: Aurora Solar (or a comparable platform) for turning a roof into a remote design and a customer-facing proposal across every lead, and a private calculator like this one for an instant, no-login check on whether an already-sized job's price actually clears cost and margin before the bid goes out. This page's own figures are a pricing model, not a roof design, an interconnection application, or an incentive determination.

This tool needs no account and no sign-in: it is a static page, the arithmetic runs in your browser, and once it has loaded it keeps working with the connection off.

Common questions

Should I use this calculator or Aurora Solar?

They do different jobs. Aurora Solar is a remote solar design and sales-proposal platform: it builds a 3D model of a roof from satellite and LiDAR imagery, lays out modules, generates a single-line diagram and a customer-facing financial proposal, and runs that design-to-close workflow through one account, on an ongoing per-seat subscription. This calculator does none of that. It takes the system you have already sized — module count and wattage, inverter and racking cost, balance-of-system cost per watt, a roof-difficulty factor, electrical and battery hours and material, permitting and interconnection, design and engineering, payroll burden, overhead, and the margin you intend to keep — and turns it into the job price, price per watt, and the walk-away number below which the job loses money, plus a printable customer proposal, instantly, in the browser, with no account and nothing uploaded. A solar company that needs remote roof modeling and a sales pipeline across every lead is better served by Aurora Solar or a comparable platform; an installer who wants an instant, private, correctly-estimated price for one already-designed job is in the right place here.

No. This site is not affiliated with, endorsed by, or sponsored by Aurora Solar. Aurora Solar is a trademark of its owner, named here only to describe what this calculator is and is not.
